tagline: Volcanic cliffs, steep grades and grass valleys along a mountain highway
intro: The Jemez Mountain Trail climbs from red-rock canyon country into the Santa Fe National Forest, with NM 4 as its main artery. NM 4 is paved throughout and predominantly two lanes; on the mountains’ east side, it descends steeply through hairpin turns with views into Frijoles Canyon. The Federal Highway Administration lists a 163-mile National Scenic Byway and suggests three hours to drive it or a full day to see it. Its account emphasizes geological formations and the area’s logging, mining and ranching heritage. The wider byway also includes excursions on NM 126, NM 290 and NM 502, extending beyond this main mountain crossing.

At Valles Caldera, that working landscape became protected land: the caldera joined the Baca Ranch in 1876, and the federal government purchased the ranch under legislation creating the national preserve in 2000. The National Park Service took over day-to-day management in 2015.

Begin the NM 4 drive at San Ysidro’s junction with US 550, passing Jemez Pueblo and Jemez Springs before the climb into the mountains. The highway skirts Valles Caldera’s southern boundary, then descends toward the NM 501 junction for Los Alamos. NM 4 continues past Bandelier’s main entrance and White Rock to NM 502, east of Los Alamos.

moments.title: Cabezon Peak
moments.text: Cabezon Peak rises nearly 2,000 feet above the Rio Puerco Valley, a basalt core left after the surrounding volcanic material eroded away. The Spanish name means “big head.” Its shape comes from lava that collected inside a volcanic cone and hardened into a massive plug. Erosion stripped away the less resistant scoria, leaving the plug exposed. Basalt columns stand vertically in its upper section and spread outward at the base; a remnant of the original cone remains at the top. The peak belongs to the Mount Taylor volcanic field, and marine sedimentary rocks are exposed at its base.

moments.title: Jemez Historic Site
moments.text: The church walls at Jemez Historic Site are six to seven feet thick at their bases, built mainly from limestone with sandstone and volcanic tuff. They belong to San José de los Jémez, the Spanish colonial mission beside Gíusewa Pueblo. The surviving structures were begun in 1621. The Jémez continued living in the pueblo and built a square kiva within the mission compound before leaving in 1680 during the Pueblo Rebellion. The site’s description identifies it as an ancestral place for Jemez Pueblo people living nearby. Wall tops have received restorative work to limit erosion, while some pueblo remains have been backfilled for protection.
moments.notice: The mission’s remnant church walls extend 110 feet in length.

moments.title: Valles Caldera
moments.text: Grass valleys lie inside Valles Caldera’s 13.7-mile-wide volcanic basin. The largest, Valle Grande, is the only one reached by a paved road. Redondo Peak rises within the caldera as a resurgent lava dome, the high point of this landscape. The caldera collapsed over and buried the older Toledo Caldera. Hot springs and fumaroles mark an active geothermal system. NASA used this volcanic landscape to train Apollo astronauts in 1964 and 1966, teaching recognition of features including ash-flow tuffs, pumice and rhyolite domes. The valley floor is above 8,000 feet, and the caldera contains a network of ranch roads and livestock trails.
